summary: A brief passage concludes the previous discussion. The Mishna then specifies how many priests participated in the morning tamid (nine) and afternoon tamid (eleven). The Gemara discusses when wine libations were offered, citing a dispute about whether water libations were used only on Sukkot. A second Mishna covers the communal ram burnt-offering, which required eleven priests, and the Gemara compares individual and communal offerings for flaying and cutting.

glossary.en: Libations; wine or water poured on the altar alongside offerings.
Ram; a male sheep offered as a communal burnt-offering.
Flaying; removing the skin from the animal sacrifice.

rashiTranslations.en: That follows neither Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov nor Rabbi Yehuda - since it counts a lottery for the fire-pan, which does not
follow Rabbi Yehuda, and a lottery for the one from the ramp to the altar, which does not follow Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Mishnah: the daily-offering is offered - it counts from the time the limbs are carried onward.
Itself - every day with nine: five for the limbs, one for the innards, one for the fine flour,
one for the griddle-cakes, and one for the wine; and this follows Rabbi Eliezer
ben Yaakov, who does not hold there is one extra for bringing up
from the ramp to the altar. On the festival - for it needs two
libations, one of wine and one of water.
In hand - one priest, one flask of water.
In the afternoon - that every day two have in their hands
two logs of wood to add to the wood of
the arrangement, to increase it; and the Gemara derives it
from a verse, that in the afternoon the daily-offering requires
two logs by two priests, but in the morning
it does not need the arranging of two logs, but by one
priest, as it is written, 'and the priest shall kindle it.'
And on the Shabbat within the festival, etc. - behold, there are twelve
in all. Gemara: from where - from the fact that it teaches, 'and on Shabbat
etc.' - by inference, that on the other days of the festival, it does not
happen to require twelve; and if you say
that even in the afternoon they pour the water libation on the weekdays of
all the days of the festival, you would find twelve in the
afternoon too - itself with nine, and two in their hands
two logs, and one with a flask of water in his hand.
And to the one pouring the water he says, raise
your hand - so that it is visible that he pours the flask into
the silver bowl on the altar, which is
perforated like a thin nostril, through which the wine flows
and exits, and that is the libation. That once
he poured it on his feet - he did not pour the flask
into the bowl but poured the water on his feet, since
he was a Sadducee and did not accept the water libation.
With their citrons - why do I need it to teach 'with their citrons'
if not to teach us that the water libation
applies only at the time of taking the lulav.
And say we do one - one priest
shall arrange two logs in the morning, as it is written, 'and he shall kindle it,'
singular, and let us do two - then two
priests shall bring, to make their two logs again
in the morning, as it is written, 'and they shall arrange,' plural, twice.
And he shall kindle, and they shall kindle - let it write both in the same
wording. Sometimes thirteen - priests occupied
with the service of the daily-offering, as we learned in our mishnah,
in the second lottery thirteen priests merit through it.
Sometimes fourteen - on the festival, in the hand of one, a flask
of water. Sometimes fifteen - on Shabbat.
Sometimes sixteen - on the Shabbat within
the festival. This is the reading: but was it not taught, seventeen -
that one is not according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov but according to Rabbi
Yehuda - that tanna holds there is also another
priest, who brings the limbs up from
the ramp to the altar, and so here there are seventeen, which does not
follow Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov but Rabbi Yehuda,
who says there was no lottery for the fire-pan; and by

necessity this tanna does not hold like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, for if so the lotteries would be too few, as we said above, and he needed a priest for the one from the ramp to the altar; and I have heard it in

other wordings, and it is not possible to establish it; and if we heard from him that Rabbi Yehuda said there was no lottery for the fire-pan, we did not hear from him that he said there was no priest for the fire-pan; rather
he says: the priest who merited the incense says to the one standing beside him, 'merit with me in the fire-pan'; but from Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov we heard that he said there was no priest

to bring the limbs up from the ramp to the altar, but they themselves, who brought them up to the ramp, would bring them up to the altar. Mishnah: the flesh with five - like the daily-offering's ramp-carrying count. The fine flour -
was two-tenths, and two priests. In what case is this said - for we need all these priests for each animal, and we need a lottery. If a priest wished to offer
alone - all of it, and without a lottery. Their flaying and dismemberment - of communal and individual offerings are equal, being valid by a non-priest, and thus it is explained in the Gemara.
This - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (on whether Chizkiyah's derivation for a non-priest's flaying and dismemberment needs its own verse) continues on 27a.

display.title: Closing the lottery chapter: one last line before the priest-count mishna
display.whats: Final conclusion of the previous lottery discussion before the new mishna.

learning.learnerQuestion: What is this brief closing line doing before the mishna on priest counts begins?
learning.coreTension: The lottery discussion spanning the prior daf needs a clean endpoint before the Gemara can move to a completely different topic - how many priests serve each offering.
learning.coreMove: This line supplies that endpoint, finishing the lottery-assignment debate so the priest-count mishna can open without unresolved business from the previous topic.

takeaway.text: A short closing line at a topic boundary is doing real structural work even though it adds no new content - it signals that one sugya is fully resolved before the next begins.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara ties up one discussion before moving to another - no topic is left hanging.
learning.learningBlocker: It would be a mistake to look for a substantive teaching in this line beyond its function as a closing transition - the lottery topic it concludes is already settled by what came before.
learning.memoryAnchor: Quick closure before the next major section.

argumentFlow.label: Lottery discussion conclusion
argumentFlow.text: Final conclusion of the lottery assignment debate from the previous page.

misconceptions.misconception: This is the main content of 26b.
misconceptions.correction: It is only a brief transition that closes the previous page's lottery discussion before the priest-count mishna begins.

quizSeeds.answer: It concludes the previous lottery discussion before introducing the priest-count mishna.

display.title: Nine in the morning, eleven by afternoon: counting priests, and proving the afternoon tamid from a doubled word
display.whats: The Mishna counts nine priests for the morning tamid and eleven for the afternoon. The Gemara asks when wine libations were offered and derives the source for the afternoon offering from doubled biblical language.
display.hint: The afternoon tamid has more priests than the morning because libations and wood-carrying require extra hands after midday.

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the afternoon tamid need two more priests than the morning tamid, and why does the Torah need a doubled phrase to even establish that an afternoon offering is required at all?
learning.coreTension: Nothing about the daily routine makes an afternoon offering self-evidently necessary on its own logic - if the Torah had only written the command once, it would most naturally be read as describing the morning offering alone.
learning.coreMove: R. Shimon ben Yochai locates the afternoon tamid's requirement in the doubled phrase 'in the morning, in the morning' in Leviticus 6. The Gemara tests this: maybe both instances of 'morning' just describe the morning offering twice, redundantly. The resolution is that redundancy is exactly the textual signal the Gemara relies on - if a single instance would already cover the morning, the second instance must be teaching something beyond it, namely those same tasks performed again in the afternoon. The extra two priests in the afternoon then trace to specific added tasks (such as additional lamp-related work) that simply do not arise in the morning service.
learning.resolution: The Torah's explicit doubling is necessary precisely because the afternoon offering's existence is not derivable from the routine's own logic - it is a separate textual requirement, not an obvious inference, which is why the derivation has to lean on the doubled language rather than common sense.

takeaway.text: When a law cannot be derived from practical logic alone, the Gemara looks for a textual marker like redundant phrasing to ground the requirement in the verse itself - extra priests for extra tasks follow once the underlying obligation is established this way.

learning.ahaMoment: The afternoon tamid has more priests not because the service is more complex - but because the afternoon also includes clearing additional lamps and performing extra tasks that don't occur in the morning.
learning.learningBlocker: It is easy to assume the afternoon tamid's extra priests reflect a generally heavier afternoon workload, when the sugya actually traces each extra priest to specific, named additional tasks rather than to an overall increase in complexity.
learning.memoryAnchor: Morning = 9 priests. Afternoon = 11. The extra 2 handle the additional tasks that only happen later in the day.

argumentFlow.label: Mishna: 9 morning priests
argumentFlow.text: The daily morning offering requires nine priests - one for each of the major tasks listed.

argumentFlow.label: Mishna: 11 afternoon priests
argumentFlow.text: The afternoon offering requires eleven priests - two more than morning due to additional tasks.

argumentFlow.label: R. Abba: wine libations on festivals only
argumentFlow.text: R. Abba: the Mishna implies that wine libations were added on festival days, confirming water libations were unique to Sukkot.

argumentFlow.label: R. Shimon ben Yochai: afternoon source verse
argumentFlow.text: R. Shimon ben Yochai derives the obligation to offer the afternoon tamid from the doubled expression 'in the morning, in the morning' in Leviticus.

argumentFlow.label: Both verses might mean morning only
argumentFlow.text: Challenge: perhaps both references to 'morning' in the verse describe the morning offering twice, not the afternoon.

argumentFlow.label: Torah's doubling teaches afternoon
argumentFlow.text: If the Torah had written only 'and he shall burn wood on it', morning would be sufficient. The doubled 'in the morning' teaches that an afternoon service is also required.

argumentFlow.label: R. Chiyya: sometimes 13 priests
argumentFlow.text: R. Chiyya: on some days thirteen priests participated, for tasks involving the wine libation (the extra two beyond the standard eleven).

argumentFlow.label: 14-priest baraita: not R. Eliezer ben Yaakov
argumentFlow.text: The contradictory baraita saying fourteen priests follows a different tanna, not R. Eliezer ben Yaakov.

theological: doubled biblical language as legal derivation
narrative: reconciliation of R. Chiyya's thirteen with R. Eliezer ben Yaakov

misconceptions.misconception: The afternoon tamid had more priests because the afternoon service was inherently more complex.
misconceptions.correction: The extra priests handled specific additional tasks (like certain lamp clearings) that happened to occur only in the afternoon - it is not a general complexity difference.

misconceptions.misconception: Wine libations were offered every day with the tamid.
misconceptions.correction: R. Abba's teaching implies they were added only on festival days, distinct from the water libations unique to Sukkot.

visualizableElements.label: 9 morning vs 11 afternoon priests
visualizableElements.description: Diagram showing which tasks required additional priests in the afternoon

visualizableElements.label: Biblical doubled phrase
visualizableElements.description: Leviticus 6's 'in the morning, in the morning' as source for the afternoon tamid

quizSeeds.question: How many priests served in the morning tamid vs the afternoon tamid?
quizSeeds.answer: Nine priests for the morning tamid and eleven for the afternoon.

quizSeeds.question: What does R. Shimon ben Yochai use as his biblical source for the afternoon tamid obligation?
quizSeeds.answer: The doubled expression 'in the morning, in the morning' (Leviticus 6) - the repetition teaches that both morning and afternoon services are required.

sugyot.finalRuling: Nine priests for morning tamid, eleven for afternoon. The afternoon service is biblically mandated from the doubled morning phrase.

display.title: Eleven hands for one ram: where communal and individual offerings part ways, and where they don't
display.whats: A communal ram burnt-offering required eleven priests. The Gemara establishes that flaying and cutting are equal for individual and communal offerings, and derives this from a biblical analogy.
display.hint: Communal and individual offerings are treated identically for the physical processing steps (flaying, cutting).

learning.learnerQuestion: If communal offerings have special rules for slaughter and blood-sprinkling, why are flaying and cutting treated exactly the same as for an individual's offering?
learning.coreTension: Communal offerings clearly differ from individual ones in significant ways - eleven priests for one ram is itself evidence of special communal treatment - so it is not obvious why the physical butchering steps would be exempt from that same differentiation.
learning.coreMove: Hizkiya grounds the equality in a direct verse-to-verse biblical comparison, establishing that flaying and cutting follow the same rule regardless of whether the offering is individual or communal, even though the elaborate eleven-priest distribution for slaughter-adjacent and sprinkling-adjacent tasks remains specific to the communal context.

takeaway.text: A single offering can be communal for some halakhic purposes (like priest distribution and possibly slaughter/sprinkling rules) while remaining governed by the ordinary individual-offering rules for others (like flaying and cutting) - status is not all-or-nothing across every stage of the process.

learning.ahaMoment: Individual and communal offerings might have different rules for slaughter and sprinkling (because communal offerings have special rules), but the physical processing steps (flaying and cutting) are identical.
learning.learningBlocker: The sugya supplies Hizkiya's textual source for the equality but does not explain the conceptual reason flaying and cutting specifically were singled out as identical while slaughter and sprinkling were not - that deeper rationale is not addressed in this passage.
learning.memoryAnchor: Flaying and cutting = same rules for all. Slaughter and blood-sprinkling = potentially different by offering type.

argumentFlow.label: Mishna: communal ram = 11 priests
argumentFlow.text: A communal ram burnt-offering was sacrificed by eleven priests with specific task assignments.

argumentFlow.label: Limb distribution for communal ram
argumentFlow.text: The mishna specifies how the ram's limbs were distributed among the eleven priests.

argumentFlow.label: Individual = communal for flaying/cutting
argumentFlow.text: Individual and communal offerings are treated identically for flaying and cutting.

argumentFlow.label: Hizkiya's biblical derivation
argumentFlow.text: Hizkiya derives the equality of individual and communal offerings for flaying from a verse-to-verse comparison.

misconceptions.misconception: Communal offerings had entirely different rules for all steps.
misconceptions.correction: Only slaughter and blood-sprinkling differ; flaying and cutting use the same rules as individual offerings.

misconceptions.misconception: Eleven priests were needed for the communal ram for the same reasons as the afternoon tamid's extra priests.
misconceptions.correction: Each offering type has its own specific distribution logic - the communal ram's eleven-priest structure is not simply borrowed from the tamid's task division.

visualizableElements.label: Communal vs individual offering rules
visualizableElements.description: Flaying and cutting: identical rules; slaughter and sprinkling: potentially different

visualizableElements.label: Eleven priests for communal ram
visualizableElements.description: Specific task assignments for each of the eleven priests

quizSeeds.question: How many priests participated in the communal ram burnt-offering?
quizSeeds.answer: Eleven priests, each assigned specific tasks.

quizSeeds.question: For which steps are communal and individual offerings treated identically?
quizSeeds.answer: Flaying and cutting - these steps are the same regardless of whether the offering is individual or communal.

sugyot.finalRuling: Communal ram requires eleven priests. Individual and communal offerings are equal for flaying and cutting.
